title: “BLESSED ARE THOSE WHO MOURN” — WHY WOULD JESUS CALL GRIEF BLESSED?
paragraphs: “BLESSED ARE THOSE WHO MOURN” — WHY WOULD JESUS CALL GRIEF BLESSED?

The sentence sounds almost impossible when your heart is breaking. But hidden inside these words of Jesus is not a command to enjoy your pain—it is a promise that your pain does not get the final word.
There are Bible verses that sound beautiful until life forces you to live inside them.
Then there is Matthew 5:4.
“Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.”
Read that again slowly.
Blessed...
are those...
who mourn.
What?
How can Jesus look at the person sitting beside a hospital bed and say, “Blessed”?
How can He look at the widow who still reaches toward the empty side of the bed in the middle of the night?
How can He look at the father standing over a grave that should never have been dug?
How can He look at the woman whose marriage collapsed after years of prayer?
At the man who cannot forgive himself for what he did.
At the believer who loves Jesus but is exhausted from pretending everything is okay.
At the mother waiting for a prodigal child to come home.
At the person reading this right now who smiles in photographs, answers “I’m fine,” goes to church, sings the songs...
and then cries where nobody can see.
Blessed?
That almost sounds cruel.
Unless we have misunderstood what Jesus means by blessed.
And perhaps that is where this verse begins to open.
Matthew did not originally record the Beatitudes in English. The Greek text of Matthew 5:4 reads:
“μακάριοι οἱ πενθοῦντες, ὅτι αὐτοὶ παρακληθήσονται.”
Makarioi hoi penthountes, hoti autoi paraklēthēsontai.
“Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.”
The wording matters.
The word translated “blessed” is μακάριοι — makarioi.
Jesus is not saying that grief feels good.
He is not calling death good.
He is not saying betrayal is good.
He is not telling grieving people to enjoy their suffering.
He is certainly not teaching the cruel idea that genuine faith means smiling while your heart is breaking.
The blessing is not found in pretending the wound does not hurt.
The blessing is found in what God promises to the wounded person who comes to Him.

The Greek word translated “mourn,” πενθοῦντες — penthountes, comes from pentheō, a word used for genuine mourning and lament. The New Testament can use this language for real grief; Mark 16:10, for example, describes Jesus’ followers mourning and weeping after His death.
Jesus knows this kind of sorrow.
That matters more than we sometimes realize.
Christianity does not introduce us to a Savior who observed suffering safely from heaven.
Jesus entered it.
He was rejected.
Misunderstood.
Betrayed.
Abandoned.
Falsely accused.
Beaten.
Mocked.
Crucified.
And when His friend Lazarus died, Scripture gives us two of the most astonishing words ever written about God incarnate:

“Jesus wept.”
(John 11:35)
Think about that.
Jesus knew Lazarus was about to walk out of the tomb.
He knew resurrection was coming.
And He still wept.
Which means knowing that God will eventually make things right does not make your tears faithless.
You can believe in resurrection and still cry at the grave.
You can trust God and still miss someone terribly.
You can know Romans 8:28 and still have nights when you cannot understand what God is doing.
You can worship while wounded.
You can believe while trembling.
You can love Jesus while your heart is breaking.
Faith is not emotional anesthesia.
Jesus never promised His followers that they would become incapable of sorrow.
He promised something infinitely better.
That sorrow would not have the final word.
Look again at the last word of Matthew 5:4:
παρακληθήσονται — paraklēthēsontai.
“They will be comforted.”
The grammatical form points to something that will be done for them.
The mourners are not commanded to manufacture their own comfort.
Someone comes to the brokenhearted.
Someone acts.
Someone comforts.
And throughout Scripture, the ultimate source of that comfort is God.
That changes everything.
Because there are wounds you cannot talk yourself out of.
There are losses no motivational quote can repair.
There are empty chairs that positive thinking cannot fill.
There are consequences of sin that cannot be erased by pretending they never happened.
There are memories that return without permission.
There are names you still cannot say without feeling something move inside your chest.
There are prayers you prayed with everything in you...
and the answer was not what you wanted.
Jesus does not stand over that wreckage and say, “Try harder to be happy.”
He says there is comfort.
And He says the mourner is blessed because the Kingdom of God has invaded a world where mourning once seemed to have the final sentence.
But there is another layer to these words.
And this one may hurt differently.
Because the Bible speaks not only of mourning over what has happened to us.
It also speaks about mourning over what sin has done in us.
There is grief because somebody hurt you.
And then there is grief because you finally realize how you have grieved God.
There is the moment when excuses stop working.
When you cannot blame your childhood anymore.
Cannot blame your spouse.
Cannot blame your temptation.
Cannot blame your loneliness.
Cannot blame the culture.
Cannot blame everybody who failed you.
And suddenly you are standing before a holy God with nothing left to hide behind.
David knew that place.
After the scandal of his sin was exposed, Psalm 51 did not sound like public relations.
It sounded like a shattered man.

“Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight.”
(Psalm 51:4)
And later:

“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.”
(Psalm 51:17)
That is mourning too.
Not merely feeling embarrassed because you got caught.
Not grieving because your reputation suffered.
Not crying because consequences arrived.
But looking at sin and finally seeing what sin really is.
A rebellion against the God who gave us breath.
And strangely...
beautifully...
scandalously...
that place of brokenness can become the doorway to grace.
This is where the Gospel becomes more than religious vocabulary.
Because Jesus did not come for people who had successfully cleaned themselves before approaching Him.
He came for sinners.
The ashamed.
The guilty.
The spiritually bankrupt.
The people with histories they wish could be deleted.
The people who know exactly what they did.
The people whose secret life looks nothing like their Sunday appearance.
The people who have failed again after promising God they never would.
Maybe that is you.
Maybe your mourning is not only because somebody broke your heart.
Maybe you broke somebody else's.
Maybe you destroyed trust.
Maybe pornography has hollowed out parts of your soul nobody knows about.
Maybe bitterness has been living inside you so long that you have started calling it discernment.
Maybe pride has disguised itself as strength.
Maybe you keep returning to something you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe there is a name on your phone you know you should stop contacting.
Maybe there is an apology you have been too proud to give.
Maybe everybody around you thinks you are spiritually strong...
but God knows how tired you are of hiding.
Then hear Jesus carefully.
“Blessed are those who mourn...”
Not because sin is beautiful.
Because repentance opens empty hands toward mercy.

Paul describes a “godly sorrow” that produces repentance leading toward salvation (2 Corinthians 7:10). There is a kind of grief that does not merely drown us in shame; by God's grace, it turns us around.
The Gospel does not say, “You failed, therefore hide.”
The Gospel says, “You sinned. Come into the light.”
Not because sin does not matter.
Because the cross proves exactly how much it matters.
Jesus did not excuse our sin.
He carried it.

“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.”
(Isaiah 53:5)
This is why Christianity can look directly at human evil without surrendering to despair.
At Calvary, justice and mercy meet.
The innocent Christ bears the judgment sinners deserve, and those who turn to Him in repentance and faith receive what they could never purchase for themselves.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Grace.
A new beginning.
A new identity.
Life.
That is the scandal of grace.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The unclean can be washed.
The runaway can come home.
The condemned sinner can be justified through Christ.
The person who thought, “God could never want me after this,” can discover that the blood of Jesus reaches deeper than the stain.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But notice something important.
Jesus does not always rewrite the story by restoring everything exactly as it was.
Sometimes we want resurrection when God is teaching us surrender.
Sometimes forgiveness does not erase earthly consequences.
Sometimes reconciliation is not immediately possible.
Sometimes the person who died does not return to our table in this life.
Sometimes the marriage does not survive.
Sometimes the friendship remains broken.
Sometimes the diagnosis changes the rest of your earthly life.
Biblical hope does not require us to lie about any of this.
Christian hope is stronger than denial because its final confidence is not that circumstances will always become comfortable.
Our confidence is Christ.
The same Jesus who said mourners would be comforted walked toward a cross.
And then...
Sunday came.
The stone moved.
The tomb opened.
Death discovered it had swallowed Someone it could not keep.
Jesus Christ rose.
And because He lives, Christian mourning is fundamentally different from hopeless despair.
Paul did not tell believers never to grieve. He wrote that Christians should not grieve “even as others which have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
There is still grief.
But now grief has company.
Hope sits beside it.
Sometimes they occupy the same chair.
Sometimes faith sounds less like shouting victory and more like whispering through tears:
“Jesus... I still trust You.”
Maybe that is the only prayer you have today.
It is enough to bring to Him.
There is an even greater promise waiting at the end of Scripture.
Revelation 21:4 gives us a picture almost too beautiful for people accustomed to funerals:
“God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying...”
Notice who wipes the tears.
God.
The Bible begins with humanity entering a world of death through sin.
It ends with God dwelling with His redeemed people and death being no more.
So when Jesus says, “Blessed are those who mourn,” He is not romanticizing pain.
He is announcing that mourning has an expiration date in the Kingdom of God.
Cancer does not get eternity.
Graves do not get eternity.
Funeral homes do not get eternity.
Betrayal does not get eternity.
Depression does not get eternity.
Abuse does not get eternity.
War does not get eternity.
Sin does not get eternity.
Death does not get eternity.
Jesus does.
And everyone who belongs to Christ will one day understand something we can only partially understand while standing among the ruins:
God was not absent simply because we were crying.
Sometimes He was closer than we knew.
Maybe you are mourning someone you loved.
Say their name to God.
Maybe you are mourning the person you used to be.
Bring that person to Jesus.
Maybe you are mourning years you wasted.
Bring Him the years you have left.
Maybe you are mourning a marriage.
A child.
A dream.
A friendship.
Your innocence.
Your health.
Your confidence.
Your reputation.
Your own sin.
Bring the ruins.
Jesus has never required polished ruins.
Bring Him the truth.
You do not need impressive Christian language.
You can say:
“Jesus, this hurts.”
“Jesus, I don't understand.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, help me.”
“Jesus, I have nowhere else to go.”
That may be one of the holiest prayers you ever pray.
And if your mourning is because of sin, do not merely feel bad.
Repent.
Turn.
Confess.
Come home.
Grace is not God's permission to remain chained to what Christ died to free you from.
Grace forgives us and begins transforming us.
First John 1:9 says that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
The answer to shame is not hiding better.
It is coming into the light of Christ.
And if you are mourning because life wounded you rather than because of something you did, do not allow anybody to weaponize Matthew 5:4 against you.
You do not have to pretend the wound is wonderful.
You do not have to call evil good.
You do not have to smile to prove that you trust Jesus.
Mourn.
Cry.
Pray.
Talk with mature believers who will sit with you rather than lecture you.
Seek appropriate help when you need it.
And keep bringing your shattered heart to the Savior who wept at a grave before commanding the dead man to come out.
That is the Jesus we follow.
The Jesus who weeps.
The Jesus who saves.
The Jesus who comforts.
The Jesus who forgives.
The Jesus who rose.
The Jesus who is coming again.
Perhaps this article found you while you were quietly carrying something nobody around you understands.
Then you do not need to perform here either.
Be honest.
Someone else may be reading silently tonight, wondering whether there is life after the thing that just broke them.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reason to hold on another night.
Do not keep this article only for yourself.
Send it privately to the person whose grief is too fresh for public conversation.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
It doesn't.

But when a ministry genuinely helps you treasure Christ, understand Scripture, reach hurting people, and proclaim the Gospel, supporting that work can become one practical expression of generosity and partnership.
But the deeper reason to stay is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is another opportunity tomorrow to open Scripture.
Another reminder when temptation is loud.
Another word of biblical encouragement when grief becomes heavy.
Another chance to put Christ before somebody scrolling alone at midnight.
Because grief has a strange way of returning.
There may come a night when you need these words again.
And when that night comes, remember what Jesus actually said.
Not blessed are those who never hurt.
Not blessed are those who never cry.
Not blessed are those whose families never break.
Not blessed are those who never stand beside graves.
Not blessed are those who have perfectly controlled lives.
“Blessed are those who mourn...”
Why?
“...for they will be comforted.”
The sentence begins with tears.
But Jesus refuses to let it end there.
Maybe that is the message your heart has been waiting for.
Your tears are real.
Your loss is real.
Your sin is serious.
Your grief matters.
But none of them is greater than Jesus Christ.
The cross tells you your sin can be forgiven.
The empty tomb tells you death can be defeated.
And the promise of Christ tells every trembling believer that the darkest chapter is not necessarily the final chapter.
So cry if you need to cry.
Repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Ask for help where you need help.
Hold onto Jesus when you cannot hold onto explanations.
And remember...
The hands that were pierced for you are the same hands Scripture says will one day wipe away every tear.
